newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn will need tricks to meet EMU-SPD's Schroeder.
newsitem.headline: Bonn will need tricks to meet EMU-SPD's Schroeder.

text.p: Germany will only meet the Maastricht treaty's fiscal criteria if it resorts to accounting tricks, Gerhard Schroeder, a leading member of Germany's Social Democrat (SPD) opposition party, said in a magazine interview.

Schroeder, premier of the state of Lower Saxony and tipped as a contender for the chancellorship in the 1998 general election, told Der Spiegel the launch of the single currency must be delayed if the criteria are not strictly adhered to.
The article was published in the latest edition of Der Spiegel on Monday.

He also attacked a French proposal to set up a stability council as a political counterweight to the European central bank, saying this would make a bad impression on financial markets and put a burden on the single currency from the start.

Schroeder frequently warns of the risks entailed in launching the euro and in December faced a storm of criticism from government politicians after he declared the euro was bound to be weaker than the mark.

Doubts about the stability of the single currency, or euro, were already leading to speculation against the mark which has depreciated sharply against the dollar as well as other European currencies recently, Schroeder told Der Spiegel.
"If it goes on like that, the Bundesbank will have to raise interest rates. I do not even want to picture what consequences that would have for Germany's domestic economy."

Schroeder also said: "I am just insisting on the promise that the new currencies must be about as strong as the mark. Germany will only meet the two fiscal criteria ... this year through accounting tricks if at all."
Countries seeking to qualify for membership of the single currency at the planned launch on January 1, 1999 will be judged on whether they meet the criteria in 1997.
Under Maastricht, nations must keep their budget deficit below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and their government debt below 60 percent (GDP).
Schroeder said that even though the Treaty allowed for a certain overshoot of the targets it was important from a political point of view that Germany met the criteria exactly.

"We have a culture of stability in Germany which is marked by the wishes, expectations and fears of those who are supposed to vote for us and who rely on us, like small savers for example," Schroeder said.

He denied he was playing on the fears of the German citizens about losing the mark. The majority of German economists and even the panel of economic advisers to the government confirmed his warnings, he said.
